Hunting for NSD exploitation attempts instead of waiting for an alert
No public exploit has been reported for the four NSD stack overwrite flaws fixed in 4.15.3, and SecurityOnline records no confirmed in-the-wild use. That absence is a reason to build detection before the code appears, not a reason to relax. entry.title: "Film look" is a contrast curve, not a noise stamp — what style presets actually change
entry.summary: "Make it look like film" sounds like a texture request. It is really four separate changes to how your pixels behave, and the difference between applying them and just stamping noise on top is the difference between a photo that reads as scanned film and a photo that reads as a filtered phone shot. Here is what actually changes, and how to tell what a tool did. Grain sits in the midtones, not everywhere. Organic film grain is strongest in the middle values and nearly invisible in deep shadows and blown highlights, because it is an artifact of dye clouds, not an overlay. A noise layer applied uniformly at a fixed opacity is the single most recognizable tell of a fake: grain over jet-black areas does not happen on real film. Highlights roll off instead of clipping. entry.title: Data Lake vs Data Warehouse vs Data Lakehouse: Data Engineering Simplified
entry.summary:
I have seen a lot of engineers think about data one way: how do I store it, and how do I query it? Data engineers ask something else: where does all this data land, and what can I build from it? That gap gets wider as your system grows. 5 services means 5 data shapes, 5 formats, 5 update patterns. Reading and writing rows is the least interesting thing you can do with them. Clean them, join them, and you get product features, stakeholder dashboards, and an honest view of what’s actually happening inside your system. There are 3 places that data can live: Data Lake
Data Warehouse
So most teams ran both. A lake for raw data and ML. A warehouse for BI. Pipelines copying between them. Two copies, two bills, and one of them is always stale. Data Lakehouse Keep the data in cheap object storage, in open formats, and put a table layer on top: Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake, or Hudi. That layer gives you ACID transactions, schema enforcement, time travel, and row-level updates. One copy of the data. BI and ML read the same tables. It’s not a new storage system. It’s metadata on top of files you already have. Weakness: you own more of the operations, like compaction, the small-files problem, and picking a catalog. Rule of thumb: I walk through all three in the full video: https://youtu.be/dRDaQ7wZHTg Over to you: is your team still running a lake and a warehouse side by side, or have you moved to Iceberg or Delta?

entry.title: Google Cloud Pub/Sub Dead Letter Queues vs AWS SQS DLQ: Handling Retries
entry.summary: Short answer: For a renewal reminder that must survive failed delivery, AWS SQS DLQ is the simpler retry boundary; choose Google Cloud Pub/Sub when subscription flexibility justifies the additional setup. If a renewal reminder must wait until a business deadline, choose AWS SQS when the priority is the shortest path to a working retry boundary. Choose Google Cloud Pub/Sub when the team needs more control around subscriptions and can absorb the extra configuration. Keep the reminder itself asynchronous: the scheduler should enqueue work, and a worker should own delivery, retry, and idempotency. That decision matters more than a small difference in per-message cost. A reminder that arrives late can be annoying; a reminder that arrives twice can undermine trust.
